- "Dangerous capability" is genuinely hard to define. Vague thresholds produce either meaningless paperwork or broad chilling effects on legitimate work.
- Poorly designed rules risk entrenching the largest labs (which can absorb compliance costs) at the expense of smaller developers and open-source efforts.
- Reported information can leak or be misused, and any single-country mandate doesn't bind developers elsewhere, raising coordination problems.

So my honest view is that the principle is sound — and it's roughly where a lot of the policy discussion has landed, including, notably, many AI developers themselves, several of which have accepted voluntary reporting or pre-deployment information-sharing arrangements with governments. The hard part is design: tight definitions of what triggers reporting, tiered thresholds so small developers aren't crushed, real security requirements for how governments handle the information, and international alignment where possible. Done well, it's a useful transparency measure; done vaguely or sweepingly, it would likely do more harm than good.
